component.name: Apache Jena
component.description: Java framework for Semantic Web and linked-data applications using RDF and SPARQL: an in-process API to RDF data in memory or in the TDB native store, the ARQ SPARQL query/update engine, RIOT parsers/serialisers for RDF syntaxes, and Fuseki, a standalone HTTP server exposing SPARQL Query, SPARQL Update, and the Graph Store Protocol over the network.

externalReferences.comment: Source security model document; this file is a structured translation of it. The source is v1, reviewed by the Jena PMC (Rob Vesse and Andy Seaborne) on apache/jena#3966.

blueprints.name: Jena and Fuseki deployment
blueprints.description: Two deployment shapes: Fuseki as a long-running HTTP server answering SPARQL Query/Update and the Graph Store Protocol from (by default) anonymous clients, with a localhost-only admin surface; and the Jena Java API embedded in-process in a trusted application. ARQ can make outbound requests via SERVICE federation and JSON-LD remote context resolution.

assets.name: Fuseki HTTP server
assets.description: jena-fuseki2: SPARQL query, SPARQL Update, Graph Store Protocol endpoints, and the admin surface under /$/*; authentication via Apache Shiro (shiro.ini). The primary network trust surface.

assets.name: ARQ SPARQL engine
assets.description: Query/update evaluation, SERVICE federation (outbound HTTP), and opt-in custom/JavaScript functions.

assets.name: RIOT parsers
assets.description: Parsers/serialisers for RDF/XML, Turtle, JSON-LD, N-Triples, and other syntaxes; parse untrusted RDF supplied on Update bodies, GSP PUT/POST, and content negotiation.

assets.name: TDB1/TDB2 store and jena-text index
assets.description: Native stores on the local filesystem, private to the owning Fuseki/JVM process; the Lucene-based text index is reachable from SPARQL via text:query and is an in-model query surface.

assets.name: Fuseki admin surface (/$/*)
assets.description: Dataset management and backups; localhost-only by default.

zones.name: SPARQL clients
zones.description: HTTP clients of Fuseki; SPARQL query is public (anonymous) by default, Update and admin require authorisation.

zones.name: Fuseki server process
zones.description: Fuseki, ARQ, RIOT, TDB, and the text index inside the operator's JVM process.

zones.name: External network and filesystem targets
zones.description: Hosts reachable by outbound SERVICE federation requests and JSON-LD remote @context fetches, and file:/http: URIs on datasets configured for arbitrary-URI access.

persona.description: Issues SPARQL queries over HTTP; SPARQL query endpoints are public by default while administrative functions are limited to localhost. The primary adversary.
Gated by Apache Shiro (shiro.ini); bounded by Shiro and dataset ACLs, with the goal of exceeding them as an adversary.
Configures Shiro, datasets, TDB location, which endpoints are read-only vs updatable, SERVICE availability, and JS functions. Trusted; out of the adversary model.
Uses the Jena Java API in-process; trusted caller responsible for its own untrusted inputs, including SPARQL injection from string concatenation.

assumptions.description: TLS is the deployer's responsibility (reverse proxy); Fuseki's bundled example setup (admin/pw, plaintext) is explicitly not for production.
The TDB store directory is operator-trusted and private to the owning Fuseki/JVM process; code prevents multiple processes accessing a single store location.
Fuseki started without a config file is read-only unless --update is passed; with a config file, only the operations the config declares are available.

threats.name: SSRF via SERVICE federation from an anonymous query
threats.description: SERVICE federation is enabled by default and there is currently no allow-list capability, so an anonymous query against a default configuration can make Fuseki issue outbound requests to attacker-chosen targets. The PMC concedes SSRF via SERVICE is a valid attack vector (not merely operator-disclaimed); operators must disable SERVICE or add egress controls on untrusted endpoints.

threats.name: Remote read/SSRF via JSON-LD @context resolution
threats.description: JSON-LD @context resolution fetches remote files by default (http/https or local file), a behaviour of the JSON-LD dependency; the W3C JSON-LD WG is working on documenting and mitigating it. Safer than XXE but a genuine remote-read/SSRF surface on any endpoint that parses untrusted JSON-LD.

threats.name: XXE or parser DoS from untrusted RDF documents
threats.description: Any endpoint that parses caller-supplied RDF (Update bodies, GSP PUT/POST, content negotiation) runs RIOT on untrusted bytes. RDF/XML external-entity processing is off by default and the recently rewritten parsers are believed safe against untrusted RDF; a parsed RDF document that triggers XXE, SSRF, or unbounded recursion/allocation would violate the claimed property.

threats.name: SPARQL operation escapes the dataset's authorised scope
threats.description: An anonymous or low-privilege query reads graphs, writes data, reaches the filesystem, or makes Fuseki act as a proxy beyond what the dataset configuration permits: unauthorised write via an exposed Update endpoint, cross-graph read, or a bypass of a configured Shiro restriction. With TDB2, FROM/FROM NAMED only resolve graphs within the dataset (URIs are graph names, not fetched); arbitrary-URI file/remote read requires an explicitly configured dataset.

threats.name: Admin surface reachable from the network
threats.description: Fuseki's /$/* admin functions are localhost-only by default; an admin function reachable anonymously over the network in the default configuration would be a CVE-class violation. Exposing the admin surface to the network without configuring authentication is an operator misconfiguration.

threats.name: Resource exhaustion by expensive SPARQL queries
threats.description: A tiny query can compute a massive cross-product; super-linear cost is inherent to spec-compliant SPARQL, not a Jena bug, and Jena is no different from any other engine here. Resource use is operator-tuned via query timeouts (server or per-dataset) and reverse-proxy request-size limits. Known non-finding.

threats.name: Code execution via ARQ JavaScript or custom Java functions
threats.description: ARQ JavaScript functions are opt-in, require explicit operator configuration of both Fuseki and the JVM, and are controlled by an explicit allow-list (eval() and similar are blacklisted regardless). Custom Java functions require the operator to add trusted code to the class path. Reachable code execution through these is by-design-operator-enabled, not a Jena vulnerability.

threats.name: SPARQL injection in an embedding application
threats.description: An application that concatenates untrusted input into a SPARQL query string owns that injection bug, analogous to SQL injection in a JDBC caller; parameterised queries (QueryBuilder / parameterised QueryExecution) are the recommended pattern. Out of model for Jena.

threats.name: Example admin credentials or plaintext setup in production
threats.description: The bundled example user setup (admin/pw, plaintext passwords, no TLS) is documented as not recommended for production; deploying it to production is a non-default-build operator choice, not a Jena vulnerability.

threats.name: TDB memory growth and on-disk size expansion
threats.description: Unbounded memory growth under continuous read/write load is a known Fuseki/TDB1 issue (the WAL guarantees no data loss on crash/restart), and a TDB2 database being far larger on disk than its input is expected behaviour (sparse files plus MVCC trees orphaning old blocks; the compaction operation reclaims space). Recurring mailing-list topics, not vulnerabilities.

trustBoundaries.name: Fuseki SPARQL endpoint boundary
trustBoundaries.description: Queries arrive over HTTP from (by default) anonymous clients. The boundary question is what an anonymous or low-privilege SPARQL query can reach: read data it should not, write without authorisation, make Fuseki issue outbound requests, read local files, execute code if functions are enabled, or exhaust resources.

trustBoundaries.name: Server-initiated outbound request boundary
trustBoundaries.description: ARQ SERVICE federation and JSON-LD remote @context resolution make the server open outbound connections to targets that can be influenced by query or document authors; the SSRF surface.

controls.name: Configure Shiro authentication and ACLs
controls.description: Put Fuseki behind Apache Shiro ([urls] ACLs in shiro.ini) and TLS before exposing sensitive data; restricting query access requires Shiro ACLs, and Update/GSP write endpoints must be Shiro-gated. Changing shiro.ini requires a restart.

controls.name: Admin surface localhost-bound by default
controls.description: Fuseki's /$/* admin functions are not reachable from the network unless the operator exposes them; keep them localhost-only or on an operator network.

controls.name: Datasets read-only unless write is intended
controls.description: Fuseki started without a config file is read-only unless --update is passed; with a config file, only declared operations are available. Make datasets read-only unless write is intended and gate SPARQL Update / GSP behind authentication.

controls.name: Disable or restrict SERVICE federation on untrusted endpoints
controls.description: SERVICE is enabled by default and disableable in configuration; there is no allow-list capability currently (a noted hardening gap; the Service Enhancer module may help). Disable SERVICE or add egress controls on endpoints reachable by untrusted clients.

controls.name: Restrict JSON-LD remote context fetching on untrusted-input endpoints
controls.description: JSON-LD remote @context fetch is on by default; restrict it on endpoints that parse untrusted input.

controls.name: RDF/XML external-entity processing off by default
controls.description: External-entity processing in RIOT's RDF/XML parsing is off by default; the parsers were recently rewritten and are believed safe against untrusted RDF.

controls.name: Opt-in JS functions with explicit allow-list
controls.description: ARQ JavaScript functions require explicit operator configuration of both Fuseki and the JVM, with an explicit allow-list of permitted functions; eval() and similar are blacklisted regardless of the allow-list. Do not enable JS or custom functions on untrusted endpoints.

controls.name: Set query timeouts and request-size limits
controls.description: Configure query timeouts at the server or per-dataset level and reverse-proxy request-size limits appropriate to capacity; this is the operator's resource/DoS lever.

controls.name: Use parameterised queries in embedding applications
controls.description: Never string-concatenate untrusted input into SPARQL; use QueryBuilder or parameterised QueryExecution in applications embedding the Jena Java API.

controls.name: TLS via reverse proxy and no example credentials in production
controls.description: Serve Fuseki behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy and never ship the example admin/pw plaintext setup to production.
